transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mrs. Kowalski, thank you for coming in to see me. I wanted to talk to you about your grandson's condition and some things that happened during his treatment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, thank God you're here. I've been praying so hard for him. He just hasn't seemed right since that medicine was given, has he? I can feel it in my spirit that something is wrong.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can tell how much you love him and how deeply you've been leaning on your faith to get through this. It is so clear that he is the center of your world.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: He is my whole heart. I just keep asking the Lord why this is happening. Is he going to be okay? Please, just tell me the truth.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Things didn't go quite right with the medication. There was a bit of an issue with how the dose was handled, and it's caused some complications with his kidneys.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What does that mean? What do you mean by an issue? Did someone give him the wrong thing?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We had some confusion with the dosing process, and unfortunately, the amount he received was too high for his system to handle.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't understand. How can there be confusion with a child's medicine? Was it a mistake? Who did this to my baby?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it feels overwhelming and frightening to hear this. I can see you're shaking. Please know that I am here with you and we are going to support you through every second of this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just feel like we are being punished. I don't understand why this was allowed to happen. Was it a mistake? Just tell me clearly.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a systemic failure in the way the medication was prepared. It’s just a very difficult situation for everyone involved.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care about the system. I care about his legs, his breathing, his future. Is he going to have brain damage? Is he going to be disabled for the rest of his life?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have to go in a moment to check on another patient, but I want to focus on what we are doing now. Right now, we are seeing some permanent damage to the renal function.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Permanent? Oh, Mary, please, no. This can't be. Please tell me there's a way to fix it. I'll do anything. I'll pray every hour of the day if the doctors can just fix this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It breaks my heart to see you in this much pain. Hearing that word "permanent" is absolutely devastating, and I can feel the weight of that grief hitting you right now. I am so sorry you are feeling this agony.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But why? How did this happen? You still haven't told me exactly what went wrong. Was the dose wrong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was some inconsistency in the calculations before the drug was administered.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not talking about inconsistencies. I'm talking about my grandson! Did someone just guess? Did they not weigh him?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let's wrap this up quickly so I can explain the next steps of the medical plan.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: How can you say that? I am asking about my grandson's life and you are rushing me!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I truly hear the frustration and the anger in your voice, and you have every right to feel that way. It's an excruciatingly painful position to be in, feeling like you don't have the answers while your precious grandson is suffering.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to know if he will ever be a normal boy again.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: To answer that, here is exactly what we are doing. First, I have already contacted the pediatric nephrology consultant, Dr. Aris. She is coming to the ward at 10:00 AM tomorrow morning to perform a full assessment. Second, we have started a specific hydration protocol and we will be monitoring his urine output every single hour for the next forty-eight hours. Third, I want you to keep a notebook by the bed; if you notice any change in his alertness or his breathing, write it down and show it to me during my rounds at 8:00 AM daily.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And the medicine? How do we make sure this never happens again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have already filed a formal incident report with the pharmacy board. Starting today, the ward has implemented a new "hard-stop" rule where two separate nurses must physically weigh the child and sign off on the weight on the chart before any medication is drawn from the pharmacy. This is to ensure that no estimate is ever used again.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't know if I can forgive this. I just don't know.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's okay if you can't. This is a heavy burden to carry. We will take this one hour at a time, and I will be here to walk through every single step with you and your family.

H.justification: The resident uses rushing language twice ('I have to go in a moment', 'Let's wrap this up quickly').

E.justification: The resident uses platitudes and hedging ('things didn't go quite right', 'bit of an issue', 'some confusion', 'inconsistency') without explicitly naming the error as a medication mistake until the patient pushes for it.

A.justification: The resident never uses direct apology language ('I'm sorry' is used only to describe the patient's feelings, not as an apology for the error) and deflects responsibility to a 'systemic failure'.

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions ('devastating', 'agony', 'frustration', 'anger') and references the patient's faith and love for her grandson.

T.justification: The resident provides specific steps with timelines (Dr. Aris at 10:00 AM, monitoring every hour), a named patient role (keeping a notebook), and a specific prevention plan (hard-stop rule).
